endorsements.quote: Faculty should play an active role in cultivating students’ critical engagement with GenAI.
To ensure ethical and effective use, digital literacy should become a foundational component of medical training [ 52 ].

This involves teaching students to scrutinize AI-generated outputs, identify algorithmic biases such as through prompt engineering tasks like “list the limitations of this AI-generated differential diagnosis,” and cross-check information against peer-reviewed sources [ 44 ].

unlisted_practices: Embed generative AI into medical curricula through faculty-mediated pedagogical scaffolding that reinforces reflective reasoning and preserves students' cognitive autonomy.
Teach medical students prompt engineering, AI output interpretation, critical appraisal of algorithmic content, and bias recognition as core digital literacy competencies.
Explicitly incorporate ethical domains of generative AI use (copyright and authorship, transparency, user accountability, academic integrity) into curriculum design and professional conduct training.
Universities should evaluate the quality, accuracy, and ethical implications of generative AI tools before widespread adoption in medical education.
Maintain continuous oversight of educational generative AI tools by academic staff, with transparency in model design and strong data governance.
Develop and implement ethical and digital literacy interventions for both students and educators to mitigate overreliance.
Conduct controlled comparative trials of generative AI versus reasoning AI on critical thinking development, and design validated instruments to measure cognitive autonomy in AI-mediated learning.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint paper discussing the impact of generative AI on critical thinking in medical education and recommending educational and governance safeguards.
